Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations (posts) in Eswatini use paper-based systems like Occurrence Books (OB) for logging incidents, officers on duty, and events; these are operational documents submitted to courts and reviewed in inquests. Recent 2021-2022 leaks confirm handwritten entries at various stations. No evidence of digital recording at facility level; case files ("dockets") are paper-based. Digital initiatives exist only at central level: Taiwan-funded EDRMS project for police (ICDF), planned Criminal Intelligence/AFIS systems (Gov Digital Roadmap), and IECMS integrating police with justice (UNDP). These central systems are comparable to those in other score-1 countries (e.g., Kenya's Digital OB urban pilot, Nigeria's WAPIS) and do not affect rural point-of-service recording. Rural police stations remain entirely paper-based.

revised_comments: Rural police stations (posts) in Eswatini continue to rely on paper-based systems such as handwritten Occurrence Books for logging incidents, officers on duty, and events, with case files (dockets) also paper-based; there is no evidence of digital data capture at the point of service. National-level digitisation efforts - including a Taiwan ICDF-funded Electronic Document and Records Management System project, the Digital Government Implementation Roadmap, an Integrated Electronic Case Management System linking the police service, judiciary, Law Society and Anti-Corruption Commission (launched August 2025), a Digital Forensic Unit tackling cybercrime, and a planned partnership with the United Arab Emirates on AI-enabled policing - operate at central, case-management or investigative level rather than at rural facilities. Frontline recording of incidents and dockets in rural police stations remains entirely paper-based.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Eswatini predominantly use digital systems for patient data recording via the Client Management Information System (CMIS), an electronic health record (EHR) system. As of the 2024 National Health Sector Strategic Plan, 71% of health facilities have CMIS, with targets to reach 95% by 2028, indicating majority adoption including at primary level. CMIS supports point-of-care data entry for clinical management, reducing duplicates and improving patient flow. A 2020 World Bank project planned rollout to 50 'last-mile' (rural) PHC clinics for real-time RMNCAH/NCD data. Digital job aids on tablets link to CMIS for decision support at PHC. Community-level RHMs recently piloted CBHIS (2026, one region) to replace paper, integrating with CMIS, but clinics separate. No evidence of entirely paper-based rural clinics; partial paper may persist in 29% without CMIS. Barriers: infrastructure, training, connectivity (addressed via APNs). National ambition (full digital) aligns closely with rural reality, unlike many SSA countries.

revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Eswatini predominantly capture patient data digitally through the Client Management Information System (CMIS), an open-source, government-owned electronic medical record. As of 2026, CMIS is live at 233 sites, covering approximately 73% of the country's health facilities, up from 71% reported in the 2024 National Health Sector Strategic Plan, against a government target of 95% coverage by 2028. CMIS supports point-of-care data entry, unique-ID based patient identification and cloud-backed record portability across facilities. A related but separate initiative is digitising community-level data collected by Rural Health Motivators through the electronic Community-Based Health Information System, distinct from clinic-level records. Around a quarter of facilities, likely concentrated in the most remote areas, have not yet adopted CMIS and continue to rely at least partly on paper, so point-of-service capture in rural clinics is mostly, but not entirely, digital.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Eswatini (e.g., Hlatikhulu, Hluti, Nhlangano) use a hybrid process: informants provide paper letters from chiefs/indvunas confirming births, officers manually fill BMD-1 paper forms, then typists enter data electronically into the National Population Register (NPR) via networked terminals. All district-level civil registration offices countrywide, including rural, have digitized databases with electronic entry of vital events across all CRVS processes (notification to statistics), advanced features like fraud detection and encryption.UNECA CRVS Digitalization ReportEswatini Vital Statistics Report 2022.pdf) No evidence of fully paperless point-of-service (manual forms persist), but digital is standard/default with paper input only. Digital backend integrated with national systems; health facilities linked via CMIS but registration at CRD offices. Low completeness (36% births) due to access barriers, not tech. Plans for further digital roadmap (2024 tender).Eswatini Vital Statistics Report 2022.pdf) Barriers: rural connectivity, training, late registrations (61%). National ambition (CRVS plan 2022-27) pushes integration/mobile units, but rural PoS remains hybrid.UNECA CRVS Digitalization Report

revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Eswatini (for example in Hlathikhulu, Hluti and Nhlangano) operate a hybrid process: informants first present paper documentation, such as chief's or indvuna's letters confirming a birth, and officers manually complete BMD-1 paper forms; this information is then entered electronically into the National Population Register via networked terminals, with district-level offices nationwide, including rural ones, holding digitised databases with encryption and fraud-detection features. Data capture at the point of citizen contact therefore still relies on paper intake even where backend recording is digital. A 2024 Digital Readiness Assessment by UNDP and the Ministry of ICT found mixed expert opinion on the extent of civil registration digitalisation, reflecting inconsistent implementation across the system, and mobile outreach campaigns continue to register rural and hard-to-reach populations using paper-based field collection ahead of later digital entry. Overall, digital capture is the norm at rural registry offices but is not yet fully paperless at the point of service.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Eswatini traditionally record administrative data (enrollment, attendance via 16th School Day Survey, termly tools), learner profiles, and support needs (OVC, disabilities) using paper forms and registers like Annual Education Census (AEC), which are sent to regional/central levels for manual entry into legacy systems.DHIS2 EMIS Report A DHIS2-based EMIS was piloted in 2021 in Manzini region (100 schools, including rural primaries e.g., Ekuthuleni, Mhlabubovu), enabling school-level digital entry of aggregate and individual PIN-tracked data via web/Android for real-time dashboards. Some rural schools entered data despite challenges, using it for planning (e.g., OVC support, meals).DHIS2 EMIS Report By 2024, MoET's national report draws from DHIS2 data collected from schools, indicating scaling.MoET Report 2024 However, no evidence confirms majority rural facilities routinely use digital at point-of-service; pilot highlighted persistent barriers: unreliable internet (weak signals, high costs), lack of school devices (reliance on personal/borrowed laptops, no tablets for offline), teacher workload/skills gaps, demotivation in rural areas.DHIS2 EMIS Report National policy aims for PIN-driven digital EMIS accessible nationwide, but rural reality remains predominantly paper-based with digital limited to pilots/early donor-supported rollout, not standard point-of-care recording.

The 2022 DHIS2-EMIS pilot assessment report cited originally was re-verified and confirms early barriers (unreliable internet, lack of school-owned devices, teacher workload) at rural pilot schools such as Ekuthuleni. The originally cited 2024 MoET National General Education Report could not be fetched (repeated timeout), but its use of DHIS2-derived national statistics is corroborated by DHIS2's own implementation page and related articles, which describe EMIS as having reached 'national scale' since 2020/2022, with a companion individual-level mobile app (SEMIS) officially launched in March 2024 and extended from an initial 10-school pilot in Lubombo region to roughly 60 schools by October 2024. This indicates continuing, uneven expansion of digital capture rather than a majority shift to digital point-of-service recording in rural schools; persistent connectivity and device barriers particularly affect rural areas. revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Eswatini have historically recorded enrolment, attendance and learner data on paper, submitted through instruments such as the Annual Education Census for later manual entry into central systems. Since a 2020-2022 pilot in the Manzini region, the Ministry of Education and Training has rolled out a DHIS2-based Education Management Information System, expanding aggregate and individual data collection to schools nationwide, with a companion mobile application (SEMIS) for individual learner records officially launched in March 2024, initially piloted in 10 schools in the Lubombo region and extended to around 60 schools by October 2024. Despite this national rollout, persistent barriers - unreliable internet connectivity, a shortage of school-owned devices with teachers often relying on personal laptops, and limited digital skills, particularly in rural and remote schools - mean that digital data capture at the point of service in rural primary schools remains partial. Most rural schools continue to depend substantially on paper-based collection, with digital entry increasingly used but not yet the norm at facility level.
